claim: In pancreatic beta cells, exophilin-8 anchors granules in the peripheral actin cortex.
source: In pancreatic beta cells, exophilin-8 anchors granules in the peripheral actin cortex, whereas granuphilin and melanophilin mediate granule fusion with and without stable docking to the plasma membrane, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about exophilin-8 function, supported by citations in the introduction (Bierings et al., 2012; Desnos et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2017; Huet et al., 2012; Mizuno et al., 2011; Nightingale et al., 2009).

claim: Granuphilin mediates granule fusion with stable docking to the plasma membrane.
source: In pancreatic beta cells, exophilin-8 anchors granules in the peripheral actin cortex, whereas granuphilin and melanophilin mediate granule fusion with and without stable docking to the plasma membrane, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about granuphilin function, supported by citations in the introduction (Gomi et al., 2005; Torii et al., 2002).

claim: Melanophilin mediates granule fusion without stable docking to the plasma membrane.
source: In pancreatic beta cells, exophilin-8 anchors granules in the peripheral actin cortex, whereas granuphilin and melanophilin mediate granule fusion with and without stable docking to the plasma membrane, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about melanophilin function, supported by citations in the introduction (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Melanophilin exclusively functions downstream of exophilin-8 to mobilize granules for fusion from the actin network to the plasma membrane after stimulation.
source: Analyses of prefusion profiles by total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy suggest that melanophilin exclusively functions downstream of exophilin-8 to mobilize granules for fusion from the actin network to the plasma membrane after stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data comparing exocytic phenotypes in double knockout cells versus single knockout cells, as shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Exophilin-8 and melanophilin are physically linked via the exocyst complex.
source: The two effectors are physically linked via the exocyst complex.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments and mass spectrometry data showing that both effectors interact with exocyst components (Figure 3).

claim: Downregulation of the exocyst component affects granule exocytosis only in the presence of exophilin-8.
source: Downregulation of the exocyst component affects granule exocytosis only in the presence of exophilin-8.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC10 knockdown experiments showing effects in WT cells but not in Exo8KO cells (Figure 5).

claim: The exocyst and exophilin-8 promote fusion of granules residing beneath the plasma membrane prior to stimulation.
source: The exocyst and exophilin-8 also promote fusion of granules residing beneath the plasma membrane prior to stimulation, although they differentially act on freely diffusible granules and those stably docked to the plasma membrane by granuphilin, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data showing effects on resident-type exocytosis in various knockout combinations (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: Exophilin-8 and the exocyst differentially act on freely diffusible granules and those stably docked to the plasma membrane by granuphilin.
source: The exocyst and exophilin-8 also promote fusion of granules residing beneath the plasma membrane prior to stimulation, although they differentially act on freely diffusible granules and those stably docked to the plasma membrane by granuphilin, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with KuO-granuphilin expression showing differential effects on granuphilin-positive versus granuphilin-negative granules (Figures 6D-E and 7C-D).

claim: Exo8KO and ME8DKO beta cells display even distribution of insulin granules in the cytoplasm without accumulation at the cell periphery.
source: The doubly deficient beta cells displayed even distribution of insulin granules in the cytoplasm without accumulation at the cell periphery, in contrast to WT and MlphKO cells, but in a manner similar to that in Exo8KO cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in confocal microscopy images and quantified in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of exophilin-8, but not melanophilin, in ME8DKO cells at the endogenous level in WT cells redistributed granules to the cell periphery.
source: Expression of exophilin-8, but not that of melanophilin, in ME8DKO cells at the endogenous level in WT cells redistributed them to the cell periphery (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1B with adenoviral expression of HA-tagged effectors.

claim: Exophilin-8 is essential for granule accumulation within the actin cortex, whereas melanophilin is not.
source: This is consistent with the previous findings obtained from cells deficient in each single effector, which revealed that exophilin-8 is essential for granule accumulation within the actin cortex, whereas melanophilin is not (Fan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion consistent with previous findings and supported by the current data in Figure 1.

claim: ME8DKO mice show glucose intolerance without changes in body weight or insulin sensitivity.
source: ME8DKO mice show glucose intolerance without changes in body weight or insulin sensitivity, as found in each singly deficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IPGTT and IPITT data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells deficient in melanophilin and/or exophilin-8 all showed decreases in GSIS compared with WT cells.
source: The cells deficient in melanophilin and/or exophilin-8 all showed decreases in GSIS compared with WT cells in both islet batch and perifusion assays, although the decreases in ME8DKO cells tended to be larger than those in MlphKO cells (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by insulin secretion assays shown in Figure 2A-B and supplementary figures.

claim: The numbers of visible granules under TIRF microscopy were not different among the four genotypes of cells (WT, MlphKO, Exo8KO, ME8DKO).
source: The numbers of visible granules under TIRF microscopy were not different among the four genotypes of cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly measured and quantified in Figure 2C using TIRF microscopy.

claim: Granules residing beneath the plasma membrane are not necessarily derived or supplied from granules anchored within the actin cortex.
source: Lack of the change in Exo8KO cells suggests that granules residing beneath the plasma membrane are not necessarily derived or supplied from granules anchored within the actin cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Exo8KO cells, which lack actin cortex granule accumulation, still have normal numbers of visible granules under TIRF microscopy.

claim: MlphKO cells showed a specific decrease in the passenger-type exocytosis, particularly in a later phase, compared with WT cells.
source: MlphKO cells with the genetic background of C57BL/6N mice showed a specific decrease in the passenger-type exocytosis, particularly in a later phase, compared with WT cells (Figure 2D and E), which is consistent with previous findings in parental leaden cells with the genetic background of C57BR/cdJ mice (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy analysis of fusion events categorized by prefusion behavior (Figure 2D-E).

claim: Both Exo8KO and ME8DKO cells displayed decreases in both the resident and passenger types of exocytosis.
source: In contrast, both Exo8KO and ME8DKO cells with the same C57BL/6N genetic background displayed decreases in both the resident and passenger types of exocytosis, while changes in the markedly less frequent visitor type were difficult to compare among the cells.
evidence: This is shown in the TIRF microscopy data in Figure 2D-E.

claim: There are no significant differences in exocytic phenotypes between Exo8KO and ME8DKO cells.
source: Because there are no significant differences in exocytic phenotypes between Exo8KO and ME8DKO cells, melanophilin is thought to function downstream of exophilin-8.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of TIRF microscopy data between Exo8KO and ME8DKO cells (Figure 2).

claim: The passenger-type exocytosis mediated by melanophilin via interactions with myosin-Va and syntaxin-4 appears to be derived from granules anchored in the actin cortex by exophilin-8.
source: Considering the previously identified role of each effector in beta cells (Fan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020), the passenger-type exocytosis mediated by melanophilin via interactions with myosin-Va and syntaxin-4 appears to be derived from granules anchored in the actin cortex by exophilin-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional hierarchy data combined with previous knowledge about effector interactions.

claim: The expression of exophilin-8 was not affected in MlphKO cells.
source: Although the expression of exophilin-8 was not affected in MlphKO cells, that of melanophilin was decreased to 59.8 ± 9.0% (n = 4) in Exo8KO cells compared with WT cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The expression of melanophilin was decreased to 59.8 ± 9.0% in Exo8KO cells compared with WT cells.
source: Although the expression of exophilin-8 was not affected in MlphKO cells, that of melanophilin was decreased to 59.8 ± 9.0% (n = 4) in Exo8KO cells compared with WT cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is quantified from immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The decrease in melanophilin expression in Exo8KO cells should not affect GSIS because a similar level of expression in heterozygous MlphKO cells did not reduce it.
source: However, this decrease should not affect GSIS in Exo8KO cells because a similar level of expression (65.4 ± 4.7%) in heterozygous MlphKO cells did not reduce it (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by insulin secretion assays in heterozygous MlphKO cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exophilin-8 and melanophilin expressed in the pancreatic beta cell line MIN6 form a complex.
source: We further found that the exophilin-8 and melanophilin expressed in the pancreatic beta cell line MIN6 form a complex (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The protein stability of melanophilin partially depends on its interaction with exophilin-8.
source: These findings suggest that the protein stability of melanophilin partially depends on its interaction with exophilin-8, which is consistent with the model that melanophilin functions downstream of exophilin-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased melanophilin expression in Exo8KO cells and the complex formation between the two effectors.

claim: Exophilin-8 and melanophilin do not interact when expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: However, they do not interact when expressed in HEK293A cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that they do not interact directly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments in HEK293A cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Exophilin-8 and melanophilin do not interact directly.
source: However, they do not interact when expressed in HEK293A cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that they do not interact directly.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of interaction in HEK293A cells, suggesting an intermediate protein is required.

claim: The exocyst complex components, SEC8, SEC10, and EXO70, were identified in both immunoprecipitates of MEF-tagged exophilin-8 and melanophilin.
source: As a result, we identified the exocyst complex components, SEC8, SEC10, and EXO70, in both immunoprecipitates, which is consistent with the previous finding that exophilin-8 interacts with SEC6 and SEC8 in INS-1 832/13 cells (Goehring et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS analysis of immunoprecipitates from MIN6 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: Endogenous interactions exist among melanophilin, exophilin-8, SEC6, and SEC10 in MIN6 cells.
source: We confirmed the endogenous interactions among melanophilin, exophilin-8, SEC6, and SEC10 in MIN6 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Exophilin-8 and melanophilin immediately interact with SEC8 and EXO70, respectively.
source: As a result, we found that exophilin-8 and melanophilin immediately, if not directly, interact with SEC8 and EXO70, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by VIP assay results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority of each effector (exophilin-8 and melanophilin) form a distinct complex in cells.
source: Although the exocyst components were found in both immunoprecipitates of melanophilin and exophilin-8, other interacting proteins such as RIM-BP2, RIM2, myosin-VIIa, and myosin-Va were identified in only one of the immunoprecipitates (Figure 3E), suggesting that the majority of each effector form a distinct complex in cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Exophilin-8 primarily interacts with myosin-VIIa displaying a molecular mass of ~170 kDa in INS-1 832/13 rat cells.
source: In addition, although we previously reported that exophilin-8 primarily interacts with myosin-Vlla displaying a molecular mass of ~170 kDa in INS-1 832/13 rat cells (Fan et al., 2017), it interacted with mysosin-VIIa with an authentic mass of ~260 kDa in MIN6 mouse cells, which may reflect a species difference between these beta cell lines.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' work.

claim: Exophilin-8 interacts with myosin-VIIa with an authentic mass of ~260 kDa in MIN6 mouse cells.
source: In addition, although we previously reported that exophilin-8 primarily interacts with myosin-Vlla displaying a molecular mass of ~170 kDa in INS-1 832/13 rat cells (Fan et al., 2017), it interacted with mysosin-VIIa with an authentic mass of ~260 kDa in MIN6 mouse cells, which may reflect a species difference between these beta cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblotting data in Figure 3E showing the molecular weight of myosin-VIIa.

claim: SEC10 knockdown did not affect the granule localization of exophilin-8 or melanophilin.
source: However, SEC10 knockdown by specific siRNAs did not affect the granule localization of exophilin-8 or melanophilin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SEC10 knockdown had no effect on the peripheral accumulation of insulin granules.
source: Furthermore, there was no effect on the peripheral accumulation of insulin granules in contrast to the case in exophilin-8-deficient cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with exophilin-8-deficient cells and the localization data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SEC10 knockdown significantly decreased the colocalization ratio of melanophilin, but not that of exophilin-8, with SEC6.
source: However, SEC10 knockdown significantly decreased the colocalization ratio of melanophilin, but not that of exophilin-8, with SEC6, another exocyst component that is colocalized with insulin granules in MIN6 cells (Tsuboi et al., 2005; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Silencing of SEC10 that disrupts the subcomplex 2 dissociates melanophilin from exophilin-8 associated with the subcomplex 1.
source: Considering that the two effectors specifically interact with the component of different subcomplexes (Figure 3D), it is reasonable that silencing of SEC10 that disrupts the subcomplex 2 dissociates melanophilin from exophilin-8 associated with the subcomplex 1.
evidence: This is inferred from the VIP assay data and the colocalization results after SEC10 knockdown.

claim: SEC8 knockdown markedly disrupted the complex formation between exophilin-8 and melanophilin.
source: To obtain further evidence that the two effectors associate through the exocyst, we downregulated SEC8 that is thought to interact with exophilin-8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and found that SEC8 knockdown markedly disrupted the complex formation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments after SEC8 knockdown shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The exocyst physically connects the two effectors (exophilin-8 and melanophilin) on the same granule.
source: These findings indicate that the exocyst physically connects the two effectors on the same granule.
evidence: This is concluded from the SEC10 and SEC8 knockdown experiments showing disruption of effector interactions.

claim: SEC10 knockdown markedly decreased GSIS in WT cells.
source: SEC10 knockdown markedly decreased GSIS in WT cells, but induced no further decrease of GSIS in Exo8KO cells, which was already decreased by half compared with WT cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by insulin secretion assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SEC10 knockdown induced no further decrease of GSIS in Exo8KO cells.
source: SEC10 knockdown markedly decreased GSIS in WT cells, but induced no further decrease of GSIS in Exo8KO cells, which was already decreased by half compared with WT cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by insulin secretion assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The exocyst functions only in the presence of exophilin-8.
source: These findings suggest that the exocyst functions only in the presence of exophilin-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SEC10 knockdown affects GSIS in WT cells but not in Exo8KO cells.

claim: SEC10 knockdown does not affect the number of visible granules in either WT or Exo8KO cells.
source: Similarly, SEC10 knockdown does not affect the number of visible granules in either WT or Exo8KO cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SEC10 knockdown induces a marked decrease in glucose-stimulated fusion events in WT cells, but no additional decrease in Exo8KO cells.
source: Consistent with insulin secretion assays (Figure 5A), it induces a marked decrease in glucose-stimulated fusion events in WT cells, but no additional decrease in Exo8KO cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy analysis of fusion events shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SEC10 knockdown in WT cells causes decreases in both resident and passenger types of exocytosis, which phenocopied Exo8KO cells without SEC10 knockdown.
source: Categorization by prefusion behavior revealed decreases in both resident and passenger types of exocytosis in WT cells, which phenocopied Exo8KO cells without SEC10 knockdown (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by categorization of fusion events in Figure 5C compared to Figure 2D.

claim: SEC10 knockdown had no effects on either resident or passenger type of exocytosis in Exo8KO cells.
source: Again, SEC10 knockdown had no effects on either type of exocytosis in Exo8KO cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the categorized fusion event data in Figure 5C.

claim: The holo-exocyst appears to function with exophilin-8 in the same pathway.
source: The holo-exocyst appears to function with exophilin-8 in the same pathway because SEC10 knockdown is expected to preserve the interaction between exophilin-8 and the subcomplex 1, as shown in Figure 4A.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data showing exophilin-8 still associates with SEC6 after SEC10 knockdown.

claim: Exophilin-8 and the exocyst mediate the passenger-type exocytosis when they interact with melanophilin on the same granule.
source: Taken together, it seems that exophilin-8 and the exocyst mediate the passenger-type exocytosis when they interact with melanophilin on the same granule.
evidence: This is concluded from the functional hierarchy data showing all three components are required for passenger-type exocytosis.

claim: Beta cells lacking granuphilin display very few granules directly attached to the plasma membrane under electron microscopy.
source: Another Rab27 effector, granuphilin, is thought to be deeply involved in this type of exocytosis because beta cells lacking granuphilin display very few granules directly attached to the plasma membrane under electron microscopy (Gomi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from previous work.

claim: Granuphilin-deficient cells display a marked increase in granule exocytosis, possibly because granuphilin interacts with and stabilizes syntaxins in a fusion-incompetent, closed form.
source: Despite this docking defect, these cells display a marked increase in granule exocytosis, possibly because granuphilin interacts with and stabilizes syntaxins in a fusion-incompetent, closed form (Torii et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism from previous work.

claim: GE8DKO cells exhibited an increase in GSIS compared with Exo8KO cells.
source: The GE8DKO cells also exhibited an increase in GSIS compared with Exo8KO cells (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), which indicates that a significant number of granules fuse efficiently without exophilin-8 and granuphilin, thus without prior capture in the actin cortex and stable docking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by insulin secretion assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A significant number of granules fuse efficiently without exophilin-8 and granuphilin, thus without prior capture in the actin cortex and stable docking to the plasma membrane.
source: The GE8DKO cells also exhibited an increase in GSIS compared with Exo8KO cells (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), which indicates that a significant number of granules fuse efficiently without exophilin-8 and granuphilin, thus without prior capture in the actin cortex and stable docking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased GSIS in GE8DKO cells compared to Exo8KO cells.

claim: The number of visible granules was markedly decreased in GrphKO cells compared with WT cells.
source: TIRF microscopy of these cells expressing insulin-EGFP revealed that, although the number of visible granules was markedly decreased in granuphilin-knockout (GrphKO) cells compared with WT cells, as expected, it was not further decreased in GE8DKO cells compared with GrphKO cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy quantification shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The number of visible granules was not further decreased in GE8DKO cells compared with GrphKO cells.
source: TIRF microscopy of these cells expressing insulin-EGFP revealed that, although the number of visible granules was markedly decreased in granuphilin-knockout (GrphKO) cells compared with WT cells, as expected, it was not further decreased in GE8DKO cells compared with GrphKO cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy quantification shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All the types of exocytosis were increased in GrphKO cells.
source: All the types of exocytosis were increased in GrphKO cells, suggesting that the absence of granuphilin facilitates granule easier access to the fusion-competent machinery on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the categorized fusion event data in Figure 6C.

claim: The absence of granuphilin facilitates granule easier access to the fusion-competent machinery on the plasma membrane.
source: All the types of exocytosis were increased in GrphKO cells, suggesting that the absence of granuphilin facilitates granule easier access to the fusion-competent machinery on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased exocytosis across all types in GrphKO cells.

claim: Simultaneous absence of exophilin-8 in GE8DKO cells reduced the increases in the passenger and visitor types to the level found in Exo8KO cells.
source: Simultaneous absence of exophilin-8 induced strikingly differential effects on each type of exocytosis in GE8DKO cells: the increases in the passenger and visitor types were reduced to the level found in Exo8KO cells, whereas the increase in the resident type was completely unaffected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the categorized fusion event data in Figure 6C.

claim: Simultaneous absence of exophilin-8 in GE8DKO cells left the increase in the resident type completely unaffected.
source: Simultaneous absence of exophilin-8 induced strikingly differential effects on each type of exocytosis in GE8DKO cells: the increases in the passenger and visitor types were reduced to the level found in Exo8KO cells, whereas the increase in the resident type was completely unaffected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the categorized fusion event data in Figure 6C.

claim: The passenger and visitor types of exocytosis are derived from granules captured in the actin cortex by exophilin-8.
source: The former finding is consistent with the view that the passenger and visitor types of exocytosis are derived from granules captured in the actin cortex by exophilin-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these types are reduced in GE8DKO cells to Exo8KO levels.

claim: At least in the absence of granuphilin, exophilin-8 is dispensable for the exocytosis of granules already residing beneath the plasma membrane prior to stimulation.
source: However, the latter finding indicates that, at least in the absence of granuphilin, exophilin-8 is dispensable for the exocytosis of granules already residing beneath the plasma membrane prior to stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the unaffected resident-type exocytosis in GE8DKO cells compared to GrphKO cells.

claim: Exophilin-8 deficiency almost completely inhibits the exocytosis of granuphilin-positive granules in GrphKO cells expressing KuO-granuphilin.
source: However, in GrphKO cells expressing KuO-granuphilin, exophilin-8 deficiency almost completely inhibits the exocytosis of granuphilin-positive granules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fusion event analysis in Figure 6D showing reduced granuphilin-positive resident-type exocytosis.

claim: Granuphilin-mediated, stably docked granules require priming machinery for fusion, such as Munc13, that converts a granuphilin-associated, closed form of syntaxin to a fusion-competent, open form.
source: Granuphilin-mediated, stably docked granules are thought to require priming machinery for fusion, such as Munc13, that converts a granuphilin-associated, closed form of syntaxin to a fusion-competent, open form (Mizuno and Izumi, 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism from previous work.

claim: Exophilin-8 can contribute to the priming process because it is associated with RIM-BP2, RIM, and Munc13.
source: Exophilin-8 can contribute to this process because it is associated with RIM-BP2, RIM, and Munc13 (Fan et al., 2017), which are known to have such a priming role in synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Brockmann et al., 2019; Brockmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the known interactions of exophilin-8 with priming factors and their known roles in synaptic vesicles.

claim: Exophilin-8 deficiency also significantly inhibits the resident-type exocytosis from granuphilin-negative granules.
source: These priming factors could nonspecifically convert even granuphilin-free syntaxins into the open form because exophilin-8 deficiency also significantly inhibits the resident-type exocytosis from granuphilin-negative granules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fusion event analysis in Figure 6D-E.

claim: SEC10 deficiency suppresses the resident-type exocytosis even in the absence of granuphilin.
source: In contrast to exophilin-8 deficiency, SEC10 deficiency suppresses the resident-type exocytosis even in the absence of granuphilin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fusion event analysis in GrphKO cells with SEC10 knockdown shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In GrphKO cells expressing KuO-granuphilin, SEC10 deficiency specifically decreases the fusion probability from granuphilin-negative granules showing resident-type exocytosis.
source: Furthermore, in GrphKO cells expressing KuO-granuphilin, it specifically decreases the fusion probability from granuphilin-negative granules showing this type of exocytosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fusion probability analysis in Figure 7D.

claim: Granuphilin-negative granules are more mobile and fusogenic compared with granuphilin-positive granules under TIRF microscopy.
source: We previously showed that granuphilin-negative granules are more mobile and fusogenic compared with granuphilin-positive granules under TIRF microscopy (Mizuno et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' work.

claim: The exocyst likely functions in directionally mobilizing diffusible granules to the plasma membrane for fusion.
source: However, these diffusible granules must somehow be directionally mobilized to the plasma membrane for fusion. The exocyst likely functions in this process, considering that it generally tethers secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane prior to membrane fusion in a broad range of cells (Wu and Guo, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the known general function of the exocyst and the specific effects of SEC10 knockdown on granuphilin-negative granules.

claim: SEC10 deficiency does not affect the fusion probability of granuphilin-positive granules that have already stably docked to the plasma membrane.
source: This view also explains why SEC10 deficiency does not affect the fusion probability of granuphilin-positive granules that have already stably docked to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fusion probability data in Figure 7D showing no effect on granuphilin-positive granules.

claim: The tethering step by the exocyst occurs within 100–200 nm distance from the plasma membrane.
source: However, this tethering step should occur within 100–200 nm distance from the plasma membrane because SEC10 knockdown has no effects on the numbers of granules visualized by TIRF microscopy whether granuphilin is present or not.
evidence: This is inferred from the TIRF microscopy data showing no change in visible granule numbers with SEC10 knockdown, combined with knowledge of TIRF penetration depth.

claim: Some granules trapped in the actin cortex by the action of exophilin-8 stimulus-dependently fuse either immediately by the action of melanophilin (the passenger-type exocytosis) or after staying beneath the plasma membrane for a while (the visitor-type exocytosis).
source: Some granules trapped in the actin cortex by the action of exophilin-8 stimulus-dependently fuse either immediately by the action of melanophilin (the passenger-type exocytosis) or after staying beneath the plasma membrane for a while (the visitor-type exocytosis) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the functional hierarchy data presented throughout the results.

claim: The exocyst may help tether granules to the plasma membrane in passenger and visitor types of exocytosis.
source: The exocyst may help tether granules to the plasma membrane in these types of exocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing exocyst involvement in these pathways.

claim: Granules transported to the cell periphery without capture in the actin cortex are stably tethered to the plasma membrane by the action of granuphilin or remain untethered beneath the plasma membrane.
source: Other granules somehow transported to the cell periphery without capture in the actin cortex are stably tethered to the plasma membrane by the action of granuphilin or remain untethered beneath the plasma membrane (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the functional hierarchy data, particularly from the GE8DKO experiments.

claim: Granuphilin-tethered granules stimulus-dependently fuse after the granuphilin-associated, closed form of syntaxins are converted into the fusion-competent, open form, possibly by the action of exophilin-8-associated priming factors, such as RIM-BP2.
source: The former granules stimulus-dependently fuse after the granuphilin-associated, closed form of syntaxins are converted into the fusion-competent, open form, possibly by the action of exophilin-8-associated priming factors, such as RIM-BP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing exophilin-8's role in granuphilin-positive granule fusion and its known interactions with priming factors.

claim: Untethered granules beneath the plasma membrane fuse stochastically after being directed to the plasma membrane by the action of the exocyst.
source: The latter granules fuse stochastically after directed to the plasma membrane by the action of the exocyst.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing the exocyst's specific role in granuphilin-negative granule fusion.

claim: Granule exocytosis is not abrogated in beta cells lacking any of the single or double Rab27 effectors.
source: It should be noted, however, that granule exocytosis is not abrogated in beta cells lacking any of the single or double Rab27 effectors.
evidence: This is observed across all the knockout experiments showing reduced but not eliminated exocytosis.

claim: Other Rab27 effectors, such as exophilin-7, can also promote some types of exocytosis.
source: For example, other Rab27 effectors, such as exophilin-7 (also known as JFC1 or Slp1), can also promote some types of exocytosis (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from previous work.

claim: Granules can arrive close to the plasma membrane and fuse efficiently without prior capture in the actin cortex by exophilin-8 and/or stable docking to the plasma membrane by granuphilin.
source: However, given that granules can arrive close to the plasma membrane and fuse efficiently without prior capture in the actin cortex by exophilin-8 and/or stable docking to the plasma membrane by granuphilin, Rab27 effectors are thought to be evolved to play regulatory roles that prevent spontaneous or inappropriate fusion in regulated secretory pathways, as suggested previously (Izumi, 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the GE8DKO data showing continued exocytosis without these effectors.

claim: Rab27 effectors are thought to be evolved to play regulatory roles that prevent spontaneous or inappropriate fusion in regulated secretory pathways.
source: However, given that granules can arrive close to the plasma membrane and fuse efficiently without prior capture in the actin cortex by exophilin-8 and/or stable docking to the plasma membrane by granuphilin, Rab27 effectors are thought to be evolved to play regulatory roles that prevent spontaneous or inappropriate fusion in regulated secretory pathways, as suggested previously (Izumi, 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the overall data and consistent with previous suggestions.

claim: There are multiple redundant paths and rate-limiting processes toward the final fusion step in granule exocytosis.
source: In any case, it is now evident that there are multiple redundant paths and rate-limiting processes toward the final fusion step in granule exocytosis, which evolved to ensure the robust performance of the mechanisms governing the secretion of vital molecules, such as insulin.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the entire study showing multiple pathways with different effectors.

claim: Multiple paths and rate-limiting processes in granule exocytosis evolved to ensure the robust performance of the mechanisms governing the secretion of vital molecules, such as insulin.
source: In any case, it is now evident that there are multiple redundant paths and rate-limiting processes toward the final fusion step in granule exocytosis, which evolved to ensure the robust performance of the mechanisms governing the secretion of vital molecules, such as insulin.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the multiple pathways discovered.

claim: Synaptic vesicles must be docked and primed on the plasma membrane prior to stimulation for successful neuronal transmission to occur within 1 ms after electrical stimulation.
source: Synaptic vesicles must be docked and primed on the plasma membrane prior to stimulation for successful neuronal transmission to occur within 1 ms after electrical stimulation (Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about synaptic vesicles.

claim: Secretory granules in exocrine and endocrine cells initiate exocytosis at a timepoint that is 1000-fold later than synaptic vesicles, even when the Ca2+ concentration is abruptly upregulated by caged-Ca2+ compounds.
source: In contrast, secretory granules in exocrine and endocrine cells initiate exocytosis at a timepoint that is 1000-fold later than this, even when the Ca2+ concentration is abruptly upregulated by caged-Ca2+ compounds (Kasai, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about secretory granules.

claim: Insulin granules residing beneath the plasma membrane prior to stimulation, and those recruited from the cell interior after stimulation, fuse in parallel during physiological glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: In fact, total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy monitoring of prefusion behavior in living cells has revealed that insulin granules residing beneath the plasma membrane prior to stimulation, and those recruited from the cell interior after stimulation, fuse in parallel, with some variability in their ratios, during physiological glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) (Kasai et al., 2008; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2004; Shibasaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous TIRF microscopy studies.

claim: Granuphilin mediates stable granule docking to the plasma membrane but simultaneously prevents their spontaneous fusion by interacting with a fusion-incompetent, closed form of syntaxins.
source: For example, granuphilin (also known as exophilin-2 and Slp4) mediates stable granule docking to the plasma membrane but simultaneously prevents their spontaneous fusion by interacting with a fusion-incompetent, closed form of syntaxins (Gomi et al., 2005; Torii et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about granuphilin function.

claim: Exophilin-8 anchors secretory granules within the actin cortex, which is considered to have dual roles in accumulating granules at the cell periphery and in preventing their access to the plasma membrane.
source: Another effector, exophilin-8 (also known as MyRIP and Slac2-c), anchors secretory granules within the actin cortex (Bierings et al., 2012; Desnos et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2017; Huet et al., 2012; Mizuno et al., 2011; Nightingale et al., 2009), which is considered to have dual roles in accumulating granules at the cell periphery and in preventing their access to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about exophilin-8 function.

claim: Melanophilin captures melanosomes within the peripheral actin network in skin melanocytes.
source: Although another effector, melanophilin (also known as exophilin-3 and Slac2-a), similarly captures melanosomes within the peripheral actin network in skin melanocytes (Hammer and Sellers, 2012), it mediates stimulus-induced granule mobilization and immediate fusion to the plasma membrane in pancreatic beta cells (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about melanophilin function in melanocytes.

claim: Melanophilin mediates stimulus-induced granule mobilization and immediate fusion to the plasma membrane in pancreatic beta cells.
source: Although another effector, melanophilin (also known as exophilin-3 and Slac2-a), similarly captures melanosomes within the peripheral actin network in skin melanocytes (Hammer and Sellers, 2012), it mediates stimulus-induced granule mobilization and immediate fusion to the plasma membrane in pancreatic beta cells (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about melanophilin function in beta cells.

claim: Insulin granules were unevenly distributed with accumulation in the actin cortex in monolayer mouse pancreatic beta cells.
source: In monolayer mouse pancreatic beta cells, insulin granules were unevenly distributed with accumulation in the actin cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Melanophilin and exophilin-8 showed a similar uneven distribution and were colocalized especially at the cell periphery.
source: In fact, they showed a similar uneven distribution and were colocalized especially at the cell periphery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The exocyst forms an evolutionarily conserved heterooctameric protein complex.
source: The exocyst forms an evolutionarily conserved heterooctameric protein complex (Wu and Guo, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the exocyst complex.

claim: In mammalian cells, the exocyst complex is assembled after separate formation of the subcomplex 1 (SEC3, SEC5, SEC6, SEC8) and the subcomplex 2 (SEC10, SEC15, EXO70, EXO84).
source: In mammalian cells, the exocyst complex is assembled after separate formation of the subcomplex 1 (SEC3, SEC5, SEC6, SEC8) and the subcomplex 2 (SEC10, SEC15, EXO70, EXO84) (Ahmed et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about exocyst assembly.

claim: In yeast, the exocyst interacts with Sec4, a member of the Rab protein on secretory vesicles, via exocyst component Sec15.
source: In yeast, the exocyst interacts with Sec4, a member of the Rab protein on secretory vesicles, via exocyst component Sec15 (Guo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about yeast exocyst function.

claim: Sec4 and Sec15 directly bind Myo2, the yeast myosin-V, for secretory vesicle transport.
source: Further, Sec4 and Sec15 directly bind Myo2, the yeast myosin-V, for secretory vesicle transport (Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about yeast vesicle transport.

claim: Sec6 interacts with Snc2 (VAMP/synaptobrevin family in mammals).
source: The exocyst components also interact with the SNARE fusion machinery: Sec6 with Snc2 (VAMP/synaptobrevin family in mammals) (Shen et al., 2013) and Sec9 (SNAP-25 family in mammals) (Dubuke et al., 2015), and Sec3 with Sso2 (syntaxin family in mammals) (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about exocyst-SNARE interactions.

claim: Sec6 interacts with Sec9 (SNAP-25 family in mammals).
source: The exocyst components also interact with the SNARE fusion machinery: Sec6 with Snc2 (VAMP/synaptobrevin family in mammals) (Shen et al., 2013) and Sec9 (SNAP-25 family in mammals) (Dubuke et al., 2015), and Sec3 with Sso2 (syntaxin family in mammals) (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about exocyst-SNARE interactions.

claim: Sec3 interacts with Sso2 (syntaxin family in mammals).
source: The exocyst components also interact with the SNARE fusion machinery: Sec6 with Snc2 (VAMP/synaptobrevin family in mammals) (Shen et al., 2013) and Sec9 (SNAP-25 family in mammals) (Dubuke et al., 2015), and Sec3 with Sso2 (syntaxin family in mammals) (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about exocyst-SNARE interactions.

claim: Melanophilin interacts with Rab27a, myosin-Va, and syntaxin-4 in beta cells.
source: In fact, melanophilin interacts with Rab27a, myosin-Va, and syntaxin-4 in beta cells (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work.

claim: Exophilin-8 knockout and SEC10 knockdown exhibit very similar defects in granule exocytosis in WT cells.
source: We then show that exophilin-8 knockout and SEC10 knockdown exhibit very similar defects in granule exocytosis in WT cells, indicating that they function together.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the exocytic phenotypes in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Neither exophilin-8 knockout nor SEC10 knockdown affects the number of granules visualized by TIRF microscopy.
source: Furthermore, neither affects the number of granules visualized by TIRF microscopy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification in Figures 2C and 5B.

claim: Exophilin-8 deficiency erases the granule accumulation in the actin cortex, but exocyst deficiency does not.
source: The sole difference is that, although exophilin-8 deficiency erases the granule accumulation in the actin cortex, exocyst deficiency does not, which suggests that the exocyst functions downstream of exophilin-8.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figure 1A with Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the pheochromocytoma cell line PC12, the nascent granules generated are transported in a microtubule-dependent manner to the cell periphery within a few seconds.
source: In the pheochromocytoma cell line, PC12, the nascent granules generated are transported in a microtubule-dependent manner to the cell periphery within a few seconds (Rudolf et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about granule transport in PC12 cells.

claim: In skin melanocytes, melanosomes are dispersed throughout the cytoplasm using the myosin-Va motor along dynamic actin tracks assembled by the SPIRE actin nucleator.
source: In skin melanocytes, melanosomes are dispersed throughout the cytoplasm using the myosin-Va motor along dynamic actin tracks assembled by the SPIRE actin nucleator (Alzahofi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about melanosome transport.

claim: Even without prior capture in the actin cortex by exophilin-8, insulin granules may be eventually transported close to the plasma membrane using microtubule-dependent or actin-based routes.
source: Thus, even without prior capture in the actin cortex by exophilin-8, insulin granules may also be eventually transported close to the plasma membrane using these routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the known transport mechanisms in other cell types and the observation that granules reach the plasma membrane in Exo8KO cells.

claim: The exophilin-8 mutant that loses binding activity to RIM-BP2 has no effect on the decreased insulin secretion in exophilin-8-deficient cells.
source: In fact, the exophilin-8 mutant that loses binding activity to RIM-BP2 has no effect on the decreased insulin secretion in exophilin-8-deficient cells (Fan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' work.

claim: The exocyst generally tethers secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane prior to membrane fusion in a broad range of cells.
source: The exocyst likely functions in this process, considering that it generally tethers secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane prior to membrane fusion in a broad range of cells (Wu and Guo, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about exocyst function.

claim: Drosophila with mutation in SEC5 displays a defect in neurite outgrowth but not in neurotransmitter secretion.
source: For example, Drosophila with mutation in SEC5 displays a defect in neurite outgrowth but not in neurotransmitter secretion (Murthy et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about exocyst function in Drosophila.

claim: This is the first study to diagram the multiple intracellular pathways of granule exocytosis and the functional hierarchy among different Rab27 effectors within the same cell.
source: This is the first study to diagram the multiple intracellular pathways of granule exocytosis and the functional hierarchy among different Rab27 effectors within the same cell.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the study.
